## Introduction

Today, most of ComEd's residential customers pay a **flat rate** for their
electricity. That means that they pay the same amount of money for a given
amount of electrical usage, at any time of day, on any date throughout the
year.

This year though, ComEd is introducing two new **time-of-use** (TOU) rates.
Under TOU rates, customers pay more for energy during the times when the power
grid is most likely to be under strain, and less when demand is typically
smaller. Electricity is expensive at times when everyone is likely to
be blasting their AC on a hot summer afternoon, but cheaper at 1 AM that same
night. This is designed to incentivize people to shift their usage to times
that create less strain on the grid.

These new rates are the product of a years-long regulatory process. Illinois's
2021 **Climate and Equitable Jobs Act** (CEJA) directed utility companies to
promote electrification and to shift electricity demand away from peak hours:
making the grid more resilient and reducing costs for customers. This
legislation created the context for the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC)
to approve both TOU programs in 2025 after extensive stakeholder negotiations
involving ComEd, the Citizens Utility Board (CUB), environmental groups,
and competitive energy suppliers.[^fn-reg-context]

[^fn-reg-context]: For a fuller account of the regulatory history, see the
Regulatory Context section of the Appendix.

Residential customers who sign up for one of these two programs have an
opportunity to save on their electricity bills. They can pay less for energy by
using it during the cheaper off-peak hours and avoiding the more expensive peak
hours. But how much money could they save, exactly? And would some households
actuallypay more?

This memo analyzes data from **smart meters** installed across ComEd's service
territory. Smart meters track how much electricity a customer uses on a
half-hourly basis, making it easy to compare the costs of the same behavior
under different rate structures.

Three questions guide the analysis:

1. Who would save money and who would pay more under ComEd's new TOU programs?
2. Would lower-income households be negatively affected?
3. If one of the two new TOU rates outperforms the other, why?

A full analysis would model how customer behavior might change in response to
changes in the rate structure. In this case, we are assuming that customers sign
up, but then continue to use electricity as usual. As a result, these are
conservative estimates on how much households might save.


## Executive Summary

We used smart meter data from July 2023[^fn-july-also] to simulate monthly
electricity bills for `{python} f"{v.n_households_jul:,}"` ComEd residential
accounts under the company's two new time-of-use rate structures:
**Delivery-Only Time-of-Use (DTOD)** and **Combined Delivery and Supply
Time-of-Use (Rate BEST)**.[^fn-commercial-names] We then compared these
simulated bills to what each account would have paid under the current flat
rate, assuming that customers kept their behavior identical across the two
scenarios. Because our simulation applies current rate schedules to 2023 usage
data, we calibrated TOU rates so that ComEd would collect the same total
revenue as under the flat rate, which is the standard practice for energy
utility companies. The geographic unit of analysis throughout was a Census
block group: an area of around 600–3,000 people.

[^fn-july-also]: We also ran our simulation using data from January 2023, the
peak heating month. A comparison between the two months is given later in the
memo.

[^fn-commercial-names]: ComEd does not propose to offer a supply-only TOU rate
option, for reasons discussed on rehearing in ICC Docket No. 24-0378.

**About `{python} f"{v.pct_save_stou_jul:.0f}"`% of households would pay less
under either rate structure.** ComEd's aggregate revenue is held constant by
construction. This means that if everyone adopted the new rates, some customers
would pay more so that other customers could pay less.

**Neither rate would disproportionately burden lower-income communities.** We
measured savings as a share of each household's total bill to account for the
fact that wealthier households tend to have larger bills. In our simulation,
lower-income neighborhoods are more likely to benefit from switching to either
TOU structure.

**Rate BEST would produce roughly three to four times larger effects than
DTOD.** Under Rate BEST in July, the lowest-income group of block groups would
save about
$`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_mean_delta:.2f}"`/month on average, while the
highest-income group would pay about
$`{python} f"{abs(v.stou_jul_q5_mean_delta):.2f}"`/month more — a difference
of $`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1q5_dollar_spread:.2f}"`. Under DTOD, that
difference shrinks to
$`{python} f"{v.dtou_jul_q1q5_dollar_spread:.2f}"`, but the trend holds. The
lowest-income group would save
`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_pct_savings:.1f}"`% of their bill under Rate BEST
in July, compared to `{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`% for the
highest — a gap of
`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_pct_savings - v.stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`
percentage points.

**Rate BEST's projected effects on consumer bills depend on placeholder supply
rates that ComEd has not finalized.** The supply charges used in our simulation
come from illustrative values ComEd submitted to the ICC last year. They are
not binding tariff rates. Rate BEST launches in June 2026, and ComEd has not
announced its actual rates. The effects we model should not be treated as a
forecast.

**Block groups in Inner Chicago tend to benefit more under both TOU
structures,** but this reflects building stock and usage patterns rather than
geography per se.[^fn-inner-chicago] Both single-family and multi-family homes
in Inner Chicago would save money compared to comparable homes on the outskirts
of the city.

[^fn-inner-chicago]: "Inner Chicago" refers to block groups falling within 25
ZIP codes along the lakefront and near downtown, running from Rogers Park south
to South Shore and west through Humboldt Park and the West Loop. "Outskirts"
refers to selected block groups within 46 ZIP codes spanning near-west suburbs
(Oak Park, Berwyn, Cicero, Elmwood Park) and far northwest suburbs (Crystal
Lake, McHenry, Woodstock, Schaumburg, Barrington, Elgin, and surrounding
communities). These areas were selected to represent a range of suburban
densities across ComEd's service territory.


## Background: How electricity bills work

ComEd residential bills have two main components: **supply** and **delivery**.
Supply is the cost of generating the electricity itself. Delivery is the cost of
the **poles and wires** that transport that electricity to your home. In other
words, you pay for both the energy you use and the cost of getting it to you.

:::{.column-margin}
**Supply** is the cost of generating power. **Delivery** is the cost of the
infrastructure that transports it to your home.
:::

Both of these components cost more at some points during the day than others. A
flat rate doesn't reflect this difference and simply charges a single "average"
price for all hours of the day.

**Time-of-use (TOU) rates** replace that single flat price with prices that vary
across different periods of the day. Prices are higher during **peak usage**
hours, when the grid is under strain and the cost of providing electricity is
high. Prices are lower during **off-peak** hours when the grid is not under
strain and the cost of providing electricity is low.

Both of ComEd's new TOU programs divide the day into four time blocks: Morning
(6 AM–1 PM),
-Day Peak (1–7 PM), Evening (7–9 PM), and Overnight (9 PM–6 AM).
But the two programs differ in which part of the bill they change from the
standard flat rate.

:::{.column-margin}
**DTOD (Delivery Time-of-Day)** varies only the delivery charge by time of day.
DTOD can be paired with whatever supply rate the customer chooses, which is
usually the utility’s default flat supply rate.

:::

The **Delivery Time-of-Day (DTOD)** program changes only the delivery side of
the bill.[^fn-dtou] Supply is unaffected. During the expensive mid-day peak
window, the delivery charge can rise to approximately 10.7¢ per unit of
electricity, compared to about 5.9¢ under the flat rate.
During overnight hours however, DTOD rates drop to about half what customers
would otherwise pay.


[^fn-dtou]: DTOD was approved in the ICC's Final Order of January 16, 2025
(Docket 24-0378). DTOD took effect in January 2026 as a voluntary, opt-in
program.

:::{.column-margin}
**Rate BEST (Basic Electric Service Time-of-Use)** is a bundled time-of-use
structure that varies both supply and delivery charges by time of day and
season.
:::

The **Rate BEST** program goes further.[^fn-rate-best] It varies
 **both** supply and delivery charges by the time of day. While the delivery
side follows the same four time blocks as DTOD, the supply side adds in
additional factors. Firstly, Rate BEST's supply side adds seasonal
differentiation (summer rates are higher than non-summer rates). Timing-wise,
supply charges obey the same logic as DTOD's delivery charges: high costs during
the peak, low ones in the off peak periods.

[^fn-rate-best]: Rate BEST was approved on rehearing (ICC Order of July 17,
2025, Docket 24-0378). Rate BEST launches in June 2026 as a voluntary, bundled
package: customers who opt in receive both the time-varying supply rate and DTOD
delivery together.

So what's the difference for your electricity bill? The more parts of your bill
that vary by time of day, the more **when** you use electricity (and not just
how much) matters. Because DTOD varies only delivery charges — which don't swing
as sharply between peak and off-peak as supply charges do — bill impacts
under DTOD are modest in absolute terms. But as this memo shows, under Rate
BEST, timing could produce big savings for ComEd customers.

:::{.column-body-outset-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/analysis.qmd#fig-rate-structures >}}
:::


## Scope and approach

We simulate what `{python} f"{v.n_households_jul:,}"` ComEd residential accounts
would have paid under either TOU rate structure, using their 2023 half-hour usage
data.[^fn-july-scope] We then compare those simulated bills to what each
household would have paid under the current flat rate to measure who saves, who
pays more, and whether the answer differs meaningfully by income or geography.

[^fn-july-scope]: We also conducted the same simulation for January 2023, the
peak heating month. Results are discussed in the Findings section.

The analysis makes the following assumptions:

- **One month, representing a seasonal extreme.** We model July 2023 (peak
cooling). The rates' effects in other seasons and annual net impact cannot be
determined from one month alone.

- **2025/2026 rates applied to 2023 usage.** For flat rates, we use the 2026
non-summer prices. The TOU rate schedules are also from 2026. These present-day
rates are applied to 2023 consumption patterns. Our findings are the result of a
constructed simulation: not a report on historical behavior.

- **No behavioral response.** We assume households do not change when or how
much electricity they use in response to TOU pricing. In practice, the theory
behind TOU rates is for the disparity in pricing between different times of day
to cause customers to shift usage away from peak hours, which would increase
their savings. Our estimates are conservative and represent a floor on
potential savings rather than a ceiling.

- **Revenue-neutral calibration.** We calibrated TOU rates so that ComEd would
collect the same total revenue for each delivery class as under the flat rate.
This adjustment is necessary because both the flat and TOU rate schedules are
2025/2026 designs, but we apply them to 2023 consumption data. TOU rates are
designed to be **revenue-neutral** (to collect the same total revenue as the
flat rate) but that neutrality can only be maintained when rates set according
to expected usage patterns for that year. Because usage patterns differ between
years, applying current rates to 2023 data creates a distortion. To correct for
this, we computed a per-class scaling factor (one number for each of ComEd's
four residential delivery classes) that multiplies TOU bills up or down until
the class-wide total matches the flat-rate revenue exactly. After this
adjustment, the analysis becomes purely distributional. It isolates the winners
and losers of the TOU structures without changing the overall revenue generated
by customer usage. In practical terms, every dollar one household saves under
TOU is a dollar another household pays more.

- **Anonymized smart meter data.** ComEd's interval data are released under
ICC-approved privacy rules that strip all customer identifiers (name, address,
account number) and apply an anonymity screen. A customer's data can only be
included if their geographic area contains at least 15 customers in the same
delivery class, and no single customer represents 15% or more of that area's
total load.[^fn-anon] Customers who do not pass this screen are excluded from
the dataset entirely. In practice, ComEd's dense service territory (northern
Illinois, including Chicago) means most customers pass the screen — though
sparsely populated Census areas are excluded.

[^fn-anon]: The anonymity screen was adopted by the ICC in Docket No. 13-0506
and is commonly known as the 15/15 Rule.

- **Percentage of bill as the equity metric.** To assess whether TOU rates
disproportionately benefit or cost certain income groups, we measure savings as
a percentage of each household's total flat-rate bill. This controls for the
fact that higher-income households tend to have larger bills (and therefore
larger potential dollar savings) regardless of rate design. Because our
calibration forces aggregate savings to zero, this metric captures purely
distributional effects.

- **Census block group income as the income proxy.** We use median household
income at the Census block group level (from the American Community Survey
5-year estimates) as our measure of neighborhood income. This captures
neighborhood-level patterns but does not identify individual low-income
households within high-income block groups, or vice versa.[^fn-bg-income]

[^fn-bg-income]: Approximately 6.6% of modeled households fall in block groups
without valid Census income data and are excluded from the regression and
quintile analyses. Household-level statistics (e.g., the share of households
that save) use the full account counts.

- **Rate BEST supply rates are illustrative.** The supply charges used for Rate
BEST come from ComEd's Compromise Proposal (ICC Docket 24-0378), not from a
final tariff. These rates have not been finalized. If the final values differ
from the illustrative rates used here, the distributional patterns documented in
this memo could shift in both magnitude and direction.


## Findings

### The distributional effects are neutral to mildly progressive

Under both TOU structures, about **55%** of households would pay less after
revenue-neutral calibration. Neither rate disproportionately burdens
lower-income communities. In fact, the data show a mild progressive tilt:
lower-income block groups are slightly more likely to benefit.

The scatterplot below illustrates this for July, when the effects are largest.
Each dot is a Census block group; the x-axis is median household income and the
y-axis is the mean percentage change in the monthly bill. The downward slope
means lower-income areas would benefit more.

:::{.column-body-outset-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/analysis.qmd#fig-scatter-stou-jul-pct >}}
:::

Under Rate BEST in July, the lowest-income quintile of block groups would save
an average of **$`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_mean_delta:.2f}"`/month**, while the highest-income quintile would pay
**$`{python} f"{abs(v.stou_jul_q5_mean_delta):.2f}"`/month** more — a spread of **$`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1q5_dollar_spread:.2f}"`**. Under DTOD, the equivalent spread
is **$`{python} f"{v.dtou_jul_q1q5_dollar_spread:.2f}"`**. All four pooled regressions (both rates, both months) show
statistically significant progressive tilts, though income explains only a small
share of the variation across block groups. The progressive pattern is real but
modest — the dominant finding is distributional neutrality.


### Rate BEST produces larger distributional effects than DTOD

Rate BEST's distributional spread is roughly four times DTOD's. The two July
maps below use the same color scale (±$7.26/month) so the contrast is directly
comparable. Blue indicates block groups where the average household would pay
less under TOU; orange indicates block groups where the average household would
pay more. Gray block groups lacked sufficient data to model.

:::

::: {.column-body-outset}

:::

On the shared scale, DTOD appears muted while Rate BEST shows vivid blues and
oranges across the territory. That visual contrast reflects a real difference in
magnitude: Rate BEST varies both supply and delivery charges by time of day,
creating more room for usage-pattern differences between households to matter.

The muted appearance of DTOD on the shared scale can obscure the fact that DTOD
does produce real distributional variation — it is simply smaller. The map below
shows the same DTOD July data on its own scale (±$2.03/month), where the
geographic pattern becomes visible.

:::


### Why does Rate BEST produce larger effects?

The difference comes down to the supply side of the bill. Under a flat rate,
every kilowatt-hour of supply costs roughly
`{python} f"{v.flat_ptc_nonsummer:.1f}"`¢. Under Rate BEST, off-peak supply
rates drop to approximately `{python} f"{v.bestec_low:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{v.bestec_high:.0f}"`¢
— well below half the flat price — while the summer mid-day peak rate rises to
`{python} f"{v.bestec_peak_summer:.1f}"`¢.[^fn-capacity-cost] That
swing creates a much wider gap between what peak and off-peak electricity costs.
DTOD, by contrast, varies only the delivery charge, which is a smaller component
of the bill and does not swing as sharply.

[^fn-capacity-cost]: The BESTECs listed here include a 1.266¢/kWh Transmission
& Miscellaneous Procurement (T&MP) charge that ComEd adds to its supply rates.
The underlying energy-only supply charge is lower. The T&MP charge does not vary
by time of day, so it slightly compresses the peak-to-off-peak ratio relative to
the energy-only rate.

The larger the gap between peak and off-peak prices, the more room there is for
differences in household usage patterns to matter. Two households with identical
total consumption but different timing profiles would see nearly the same bill
under DTOD, because the delivery spread is modest. Under Rate BEST, the same
timing difference would produce a meaningful gap in bills — and because the
analysis is revenue-neutral, that gap shows up as a wider distributional spread.

:::{.callout-important}
## Rate BEST's supply rates are illustrative

The supply charges used for Rate BEST in this analysis come from ComEd's
Compromise Proposal (ICC Docket 24-0378), not from a final tariff. ComEd has not
announced the actual supply rates for Rate BEST's June 2026 launch. If the final
off-peak supply rates differ materially from the illustrative values used here,
both the magnitude and direction of the distributional effects documented in this
memo could change.
:::


### The progressive tilt is strongest in summer

The distributional effects are three to four times larger in July than in
January across both rate structures.

Under Rate BEST in July, the lowest-income quintile of block groups would save
**`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** of their bill on average,
compared to **`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`%** for the
highest-income quintile — a gap of
**`{python} f"{v.stou_jul_q1_pct_savings - v.stou_jul_q5_pct_savings:.1f}"`
percentage points**.


### January: same pattern, smaller effects

The January simulation tells the same directional story at a smaller scale.
About **`{python} f"{v.pct_save_stou_jan:.0f}"`%** of households would pay less
under Rate BEST and **`{python} f"{v.pct_save_dtou_jan:.0f}"`%** under DTOD —
similar shares to July but with much smaller dollar amounts at stake.

The progressive tilt persists but is muted. Under DTOD in January, the
lowest-income quintile of block groups would save
**`{python} f"{v.dtou_jan_q1_pct:.2f}"`%** of their bill, compared to
**`{python} f"{v.dtou_jan_q5_pct:.2f}"`%** for the highest-income quintile — a
gap of just **`{python} f"{v.dtou_jan_q1q5_gap:.1f}"` percentage points**. Under
Rate BEST, percentage savings hover around
**`{python} f"{v.stou_jan_mean_pct:.1f}"`%** across all income quintiles with no
meaningful spread, though the pooled regression remains statistically significant
(p < 0.001). The progressive gradient is real in both cases but too small to
have practical policy significance in any single winter month.

The two January maps below use the same layout and color conventions as the July
maps, on a shared ±$2.97/month scale. Blue indicates block groups where the
average household would pay less under TOU; orange indicates block groups where
the average household would pay more.

::: {.column-body-outset}
<iframe width="100%" height="500" frameborder="0" title="DTOD January" src="FELT_URL_DTOD_JAN"></iframe>
:::

::: {.column-body-outset}
<iframe width="100%" height="500" frameborder="0" title="Rate BEST January" src="FELT_URL_STOU_JAN"></iframe>
:::

One likely explanation for the seasonal difference is air conditioning. Summer
cooling pushes more consumption into the expensive mid-day peak window (1–7 PM),
and that peak exposure may correlate with income — higher-income households tend
to live in larger single-family homes with more cooling capacity. In winter,
electric heating loads are more evenly distributed across the day, compressing
the gap between peak and off-peak consumption and leaving less room for
income-correlated usage patterns to produce distributional differences. We do not
have direct evidence for this causal mechanism in our data, but it is consistent
with the seasonal pattern we observe.


### Geographic patterns: why does Inner Chicago benefit more?

::: {.column-body-outset}
<iframe width="100%" height="500" frameborder="0" title="Rate BEST July (Chicago detail)" src="FELT_URL_STOU_JUL_CHICAGO"></iframe>
:::

Inner Chicago block groups tend to show larger benefits under both TOU
structures. The pattern reflects building stock and usage patterns rather than
geography per se.

Roughly **`{python} f"{v.core_chicago_mf_share*100:.0f}"`%** of accounts in
Inner Chicago are multi-family (delivery class C24), compared to
**`{python} f"{v.suburban_mf_share*100:.0f}"`%** in surrounding areas on the
outskirts of the city.[^fn-delivery-classes] Multi-family households use less
electricity overall and concentrate less of their consumption in the expensive
Mid-Day Peak window. Under TOU pricing, that usage pattern translates into
larger savings.

[^fn-delivery-classes]: ComEd assigns residential customers to "delivery
classes" based on their building type and heating source. The two largest
classes are C23 (single-family homes without electric heat) and C24
(multi-family buildings without electric heat). Each class has its own
per-kilowatt-hour (kWh) delivery rate — the charge for each unit of electricity
delivered to the customer. Under the current flat rate, C23 customers pay
6.228¢/kWh for delivery, while C24 customers pay 4.791¢/kWh. A kilowatt-hour is
the standard unit for measuring electricity consumption: approximately the
energy used by running ten 100-watt light bulbs for one hour.

But the pattern holds even within single-family homes. C23 households in Inner
Chicago would save **$`{python} f"{v.core_chicago_sf_mean_stou_jul:.2f}"`** per
month under Rate BEST in July, compared to a
**$`{python} f"{v.suburban_sf_mean_stou_jul:.2f}"`** increase for C23 households
in the outskirts. Urban single-family homes likely have smaller footprints, less
air conditioning capacity, and more shading from adjacent structures — all of
which reduce peak-hour consumption and produce larger benefits under TOU
pricing.


## The bottom line

The distributional effects of both TOU rate structures are neutral to mildly
progressive. Lower-income communities are not disproportionately burdened — they
are slightly more likely to benefit. Rate BEST produces larger distributional
effects than DTOD, but both the magnitude and direction of that pattern depend on
illustrative supply rates that ComEd has not yet finalized.


## Appendix {.appendix}

### Data and Methods

This section describes the data sources, transformations, and assumptions
underlying each major finding in sufficient detail to reproduce the analysis.

#### Smart meter data

**Source:** ComEd Anonymous Data Service, accessed under the ICC-approved
privacy framework (Docket No. 13-0506). The dataset provides half-hourly
interval energy consumption (48 readings per day) for residential customers with
AMI meters, anonymized under the 15/15 Rule.

**Months modeled:** January 2023 and July 2023.

**Account counts:**

| Month | Accounts in raw data | Accounts in Block Group-level analysis |
|-------|---------------------|-------------------------------|
| January 2023 | `{python} f"{v.n_households_jan:,}"` | `{python} f"{v.n_bg_analysis_jan:,}"` |
| July 2023 | `{python} f"{v.n_households_jul:,}"` | `{python} f"{v.n_bg_analysis_jul:,}"` |

The difference between raw and Block Group-level counts reflects two filters:
(1) an inner join to the account-to-block-group crosswalk, which drops
approximately 0.04% of accounts with no block group match, and (2) a Census
income filter that excludes block groups with null or invalid median household
income. Approximately 6.6% of modeled households fall in block groups without
valid income data and are excluded from regressions and quintile
analyses. Household-level statistics (e.g., share saving) use the full raw
counts.

**Delivery classes included:** C23 (single-family, no electric space heat), C24
(multi-family, no electric space heat), C26 (single-family,
electric space heat), C28 (multi-family, electric space heat). Classes C25
(dusk-to-dawn/outdoor lighting) and C27 (electric heating with thermal storage)
are excluded throughout because ComEd publishes no TOU delivery facility charges
for these non-standard residential classes. Without published rates, no bill
comparison can be computed.

**Anonymization constraints:** Account identifiers are regenerated each month.
There is no persistent ID linking a household's January record to its July
record. Each month is analyzed as an independent cross-section.

**Data pipeline:** Raw CSVs were converted to Parquet format, with naming
convention `YYYY/MM/part-NNNNN.parquet`. Conversion resulted in files
approximately 1 GiB in size. All 49 months of available data were restructured
and verified, though only January and July 2023 are used in this analysis.


#### Geographic crosswalk

**Source:** A ZIP+4-to-Census-block crosswalk was purchased from Melissa, a
commercial data firm. Census blocks were then aggregated to block groups in a
subsequent pipeline stage.

**Match rate:** 1.34 million accounts matched to 4,840 block groups, with a
99.97% match rate.

**Income data:** Median household income at the block group level is drawn from
the American Community Survey 2023 5-year estimates.

| Statistic | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Mean Block Group median income | $96,345 |
| Median Block Group median income | $88,710 |
| Minimum | $2,500 |
| Maximum | $250,002 (Census top-code) |
| Total Block Groups with data (Jan) | `{python} f"{v.n_bgs_jan:,}"` |
| Total Block Groups with data (Jul) | `{python} f"{v.n_bgs_jul:,}"` |


#### Bill calculation

For each household and each month, three bills are computed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Flat bill} &= \text{PTC}_{\text{flat}} \times \text{kWh}_{\text{total}} + \text{DFC}_{\text{flat}} \times \text{kWh}_{\text{total}} \\
\text{DTOD bill} &= \text{PTC}_{\text{flat}} \times \text{kWh}_{\text{total}} + \sum_{p} \text{DFC}_{\text{TOU}}^{(p)} \times \text{kWh}^{(p)} \\
\text{Rate BEST bill} &= \sum_{p} \text{BESTEC}^{(p)} \times \text{kWh}^{(p)} + \sum_{p} \text{DFC}_{\text{TOU}}^{(p)} \times \text{kWh}^{(p)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Sign convention:** `delta = flat bill − alternative bill`. Positive delta means
the customer saves money under TOU.

The four TOU time periods are: Morning (6 AM–1 PM), Mid-Day Peak (1–7 PM),
Evening (7–9 PM), Overnight (9 PM–6 AM). These apply year-round for delivery.
Supply periods under Rate BEST additionally vary by season (summer: June–
September; non-summer: October–May).


#### Revenue-neutral calibration

To isolate distributional effects from rate-vintage artifacts, we apply a
per-delivery-class revenue-neutrality scalar. For each delivery class, the scalar
is computed as:

$$
\text{scalar}_c = \frac{\sum_{i \in c} \text{flat bill}_i}{\sum_{i \in c} \text{TOU bill}_i}
$$

Each household's TOU bill is multiplied by the scalar for its delivery class
before computing deltas. This forces total TOU revenue to equal total flat
revenue within each class, so the resulting bill changes reflect only
distributional differences — who benefits and who pays more relative to other
customers — not whether bills go up or down overall.

This is a modeling choice, not a regulatory finding. It ensures that the analysis
is purely distributional, but the scalars do not represent any rate approved or
proposed by the ICC.

#### Equity analysis: regressions

**Method:** OLS regression of block-group-level mean percentage savings on
block-group median household income, with HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent)
robust standard errors.

**Specification:**
`mean_pct_savings = β₀ + β₁ × (median_income / 10000) + ε`

Income is scaled by $10,000 so that β₁ represents the change in percentage
savings per $10,000 increase in block-group median income. A negative β₁
indicates a progressive pattern. A positive β₁ indicates a regressive pattern.

**Groupings:** Regressions were run for each of 4 scenarios (2 rate structures ×
2 months) across 5 class groupings (pooled + 4 individual delivery classes), for
a total of 40 regressions. All 40 were independently reproduced from the raw
Block Group-level CSVs with exact numerical agreement.

**Key pooled results (percentage savings):**

| Scenario | β₁ (per $10K) | p-value | R² | Interpretation |
|----------|--------------|---------|-----|---------------|
| Rate BEST Jul | −0.214 | <0.001 | 5.3% | Progressive |
| DTOD Jul | −0.059 | <0.001 | 5.4% | Progressive |
| Rate BEST Jan | −0.060 | <0.001 | 1.0% | Progressive |
| DTOD Jan | −0.014 | <0.001 | 0.8% | Progressive |

The complete 40-regression table, including per-class results and
absolute-dollar regressions, is available in the project repository.

#### Choropleth maps

**Platform:** Felt (felt.com).

**Data preparation:** Block-group-level mean deltas are clamped and exported as
GeoJSON. The pipeline's sign convention is `delta = flat − TOU` (positive =
customer saves). Felt's default diverging color ramp maps high values to red. To
align red with "pays more," the map field is inverted:
`cost_change = -mean_delta_clamped`. This way blue = saves and red = pays more,
matching intuitive expectations.

**Color range:** ±$25.45, computed as the 80th percentile of |mean_delta| across
all 20 scenario files. This symmetric bound ensures cross-map comparability.

**Domain anchoring:** Before upload, a script injects two synthetic GeoJSON
features with `cost_change` set to ±$25.45 and `n_households = 0` to force
Felt's color ramp to use the full symmetric range and center on zero.


#### Limitations

1. **Two months do not capture full annual impacts.** Shoulder months likely
show smaller bill impacts. The annual net equity effect cannot be determined
from January and July alone.

2. **No behavioral response modeled.** Some households would shift load in
response to TOU pricing, increasing their savings. Our estimates represent a
floor.

3. **Block-group-level income proxy.** Within-Block Group income heterogeneity
is not captured. Individual low-income households in high-income Block Groups
are not separately identified.

4. **Census income top-coding.** Approximately 40 Block Groups have median
income at or near $250,001, understating true income and potentially
attenuating the estimated income gradient.

5. **Small-sample delivery classes.** C26 and C28 regressions have 282–341 Block
Groups and limited statistical power. Results for these classes are directional
only.

6. **Rate vintage mixing.** Supply uses 2025/2026 flat PTCs; delivery uses 2026
flat and TOU DFCs; Rate BEST BESTECs are illustrative from the Compromise Proposal.
The analysis applies these rates to 2023 usage patterns.

7. **Rate BEST supply rates are not final.** Both the direction and magnitude of
Rate BEST findings depend on the actual supply rates ComEd sets for the June
2026 launch.

8. **Revenue-neutral calibration isolates distributional effects but does not
predict actual bill changes.** The per-class scalars ensure aggregate revenue
equality within each delivery class but do not represent a regulatory finding or
a forecast of realized bills.


### Regulatory context

ComEd's TOU rates are the product of a multi-year legislative and regulatory
process rooted in the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA, P.A. 102-0662),
signed into law on September 15, 2021. Among many other provisions, CEJA
required Illinois utility companies to file Beneficial Electrification (BE)
Plans to promote vehicle electrification and grid flexibility. ComEd's first BE
Plan was approved in March 2023 (ICC Docket 22-0432/22-0442), and that order
directed ComEd to propose a residential TOU delivery rate.

The proceeding, ICC Docket 24-0378, was filed by ComEd in May 2024. Its
statutory scope was narrow: to reallocate ComEd's delivery service revenue
requirement among customer classes on a revenue-neutral basis. The ICC's Final
Order (January 16, 2025) approved the Delivery Time-of-Day (DTOD) rate as a
voluntary, opt-in program with four time blocks. The Commission initially
declined to approve a supply-side TOU rate, citing competitive market concerns
that had not been fully litigated.

ComEd petitioned for rehearing to obtain approval for a combined
supply-and-delivery TOU rate. The ICC granted rehearing on March 6, 2025. After
stakeholder negotiations involving ComEd, CUB, the Environmental Defense Fund
(EDF), and others, the Commission approved Rate BEST in its Order on Rehearing
(July 17, 2025). Rate BEST uses the same four time blocks as DTOD and is
available only bundled with DTOD.
